title: What NGOs and rights groups told UK officials about Bangladesh’s political climate
excerpt: A UK Home Office fact-finding report, based on June interviews in Dhaka, records more freedom for civil society but pressure from regulators and concern over detention.
content:
The UK Home Office has published a fact-finding report on Bangladesh’s political situation, based on interviews in Dhaka from 7 to 15 June 2026. It was produced by the Country Policy and Information Team of UK Visas and Immigration, with support from the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, and first published on 14 October.

Reports like this feed into UK decisions on asylum claims, so they are read closely by lawyers, researchers and rights groups.

Who was interviewed

The team met 24 people from 15 sources: members of parliament from the BNP, Jamaat-e-Islami and NCP; an international NGO; human rights organisations including Ain O Salish Kendra (ASK); SHUJAN; the Campaign for Popular Education (CAMPE); the BRAC Institute of Governance and Development; a journalist; a victims’ network; and Bangladesh Police.

What they said

  • More space: civil society and rights groups “reported greater freedom to operate, express views and engage in public debate” than under the former Awami League government.
  • Pressure from regulators: one NGO source said: “When the regulator calls and asks us to do something, we feel pressure.” This referred to requests to campaign for the referendum.
  • Online expression: one source said the BNP government had introduced some barriers to online expression. An analyst warned that if arrests of activists and journalists rise, “the government statements will not match their actions.”
  • Political violence “continues to occur, but is generally localised,” mostly over local influence, business and resources. Sources described the 2026 election as generally peaceful.
  • Detention: rights activists were “concerned about detention without trial, prolonged detention,” and raised torture and the death penalty in some cases. They said enforced disappearances had fallen sharply, with one suspected case since 2024.

The report presents these as sources’ views from interviews, not verified findings, and advises readers to weigh them against other evidence.

Why it matters

The report is one of the few published accounts of how NGOs themselves describe the operating climate under the new government. The comment about regulators asking NGOs to campaign is a warning sign for organisations that depend on NGO Affairs Bureau approvals. Read alongside the draft cyber law amendments, it suggests civic space is wider than before 2024 but not secure.

What to watch

Whether the UK updates its country guidance for Bangladesh on the basis of this report, and whether Bangladeshi NGO networks publish their own assessments of civic space.

Sources

  • Report of a fact-finding mission: Bangladesh, political situation, October 2026, UK Home Office, first published 14 October 2026
